record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Appendix D contains noisy generated samples, but this does not prevent reading the scaling-law results.
record.tranche_reason: It reports scaling-law and compute-optimal-allocation results for likelihood-based diffusion language models, a new training/modeling regime compared with the autoregressive scaling laws in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper tests held-out likelihood scaling with compute and compute-optimal model size. It does not report a direct predicted-versus-observed validation of extrapolation from smaller runs. The benchmark likelihoods and the human sample-quality comparison are not scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study runs IsoFLOP scaling analyses (1e16–1e19 non-embedding FLOPs) for likelihood-trained diffusion language models and matched autoregressive baselines. It fits compute-optimal loss and parameter-size power laws, so its own results bear on V1 and V3 in a new model class. It also has text-only results on V2 (Plaid 1B against the curve) and V4 (depth sensitivity).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors also conclude that Plaid 1B, trained using the scaling analysis, beats GPT-2 124M in zero-shot likelihood on six benchmarks. They frame the 64× efficiency gap as a tractable open problem.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an IsoFLOP analysis and fits compute-optimal loss and parameter-size scaling laws, but applies them to likelihood-based diffusion language models. FLOP counts exclude embedding layers and output projections.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says its autoregressive scaling law differs slightly from Hoffmann et al. because embedding-layer and output-projection FLOPs are excluded.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal compute, compute-optimal diffusion LMs are about 4× smaller than AR models and need about 64× more compute for equal loss, a constant offset across scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law exponents transfer across generative model classes (diffusion vs autoregressive), but constant factors and the compute-optimal size offset do not, so AR allocation rules misallocate compute for other model classes.

record.problems: Scaling-law exponents and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text. The paper reports that quadratic fits approximate the data well, but does not provide a direct predicted-versus-observed validation for runs beyond the fit range. Its autoregressive scaling result is affected by excluding embedding and output-projection FLOPs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law results reported. Benchmark comparisons and sample-quality results were left out because they do not measure the scaling relations in the claim.

untested.parts: Separate loss scaling in parameters or tokens with the other factors non-limiting. Only the compute-optimal frontier is fitted.
No quantitative predicted-versus-observed error for runs beyond the fit range.
Numerical exponents and a separate token-count law are not reported.
Not tested: no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Not tested: the benchmark perplexities are zero-shot likelihoods, not downstream task scaling.
Fitting method, schedule and data are not varied. The FLOP-counting effect is asserted, not quantified.

missing.what: Plaid 1B (1.3B params, 314B tokens, 2.5e21 FLOPs) plotted against the Plaid loss law fitted at 1e16–1e19, a qualitative extrapolation check
Plaid performance increases significantly with depth up to ~16 layers and is sensitive to embedding dimension, contrasted with AR insensitivity to aspect ratio
The 64× constant compute-efficiency gap between Plaid and AR at equal loss

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. No exponents or fit uncertainties are reported; quadratic IsoFLOP fits are described as approximating the data well. Batch sizes, aspect ratios and weight decay were set by heuristics and learning rates by µTransfer, which may affect the comparisons. The depth sensitivity for V4 is a diffusion-specific design observation with no reported numbers.

versions.untested_parts: Tests compute-optimal held-out loss against compute; it does not independently test loss scaling with parameters or tokens while the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No direct comparison of loss predictions from smaller runs with observed losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Reports compute-optimal model-size trends, but does not state numerical exponents or separately establish how token count grows with compute.
No controlled comparison of architectures at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law test in other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No test of downstream-task performance scaling or its predictability from pretraining loss.
Shows that the autoregressive scaling law differs slightly with the FLOP-counting convention; does not systematically vary fitting method, training schedule, or data.
